reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases / Manson's Tropical Diseases
clinicalPearls: Carrion disease is caused by Bartonella bacilliformis and is transmitted by sandflies (Lutzomyia species) in the Andean valleys of Peru, Ecuador and Colombia
The illness is classically biphasic: an acute haematic phase (Oroya fever) followed weeks to months later by a chronic eruptive phase (verruga peruana)

Oroya fever is an acute febrile illness with severe haemolytic anaemia caused by intra-erythrocytic bacteria, and carries high mortality if untreated, often compounded by secondary infections such as Salmonella
Verruga peruana is characterised by crops of red-purple vascular skin nodules (angiomatous papules) that can resemble pyogenic granulomas or bacillary angiomatosis
Diagnosis in the acute phase uses peripheral blood smear showing bacilli within red cells and blood culture; the eruptive phase is supported by histology of skin lesions and serology or PCR
Asymptomatic carriage occurs and sustains transmission, and immunity after infection modifies the presentation in endemic residents versus travellers
Treatment differs by phase, using antibiotics effective against Bartonella; severe Oroya fever requires cover for concurrent bacteraemias and supportive transfusion
reference.pathophysiology: Bartonella bacilliformis is inoculated during the bite of an infected sandfly. The bacterium invades and multiplies within erythrocytes, causing massive intravascular and extravascular haemolysis that produces the profound anaemia of the acute Oroya fever phase; immunosuppression during this phase predisposes to superimposed infections. After the acute illness resolves the organism persists and, in the eruptive phase, stimulates vascular endothelial proliferation, producing the angiomatous cutaneous nodules of verruga peruana. Cell-mediated immunity governs progression between phases, and partial immunity in endemic populations attenuates disease.
additionalDifferentials: Malaria and other causes of febrile haemolytic anaemia
Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella henselae/quintana, especially in HIV)
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood smear for intra-erythrocytic bacilli in the acute phase
Blood cultures (including for secondary pathogens such as Salmonella)
Full blood count and haemolysis markers documenting anaemia
Skin biopsy and histology of eruptive lesions showing endothelial proliferation
Serology and PCR for Bartonella bacilliformis where available
Screening for co-infection given immunosuppression in the acute phase
redFlags: Severe haemolytic anaemia with haemodynamic compromise in Oroya fever
Signs of secondary bacteraemia or sepsis (e.g. Salmonella)
Profound immunosuppression during the acute phase
Failure to improve on antibiotics suggesting concurrent infection
reference.prognosis: Untreated Oroya fever has a high mortality from haemolysis and secondary infection, whereas prompt antibiotic and supportive treatment greatly improves survival; the eruptive verruga phase is generally benign and self-limiting though lesions can bleed and persist.
pitfalls: Attributing febrile haemolysis to malaria alone and missing the blood-smear bacilli
Overlooking secondary Salmonella or other bacteraemia in acute-phase patients
Mistaking verruga peruana nodules for pyogenic granuloma, Kaposi sarcoma or bacillary angiomatosis
Using the same treatment approach for both phases without accounting for their differences
Underestimating transfusion and supportive needs in severe anaemia
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Antibiotic therapy for Oroya fever, historically chloramphenicol and now commonly a fluoroquinolone such as ciprofloxacin or a beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone
Blood transfusion and supportive care for the severe haemolytic anaemia of the acute phase
Empirical cover for secondary infections such as Salmonella during the immunosuppressed acute phase
Azithromycin or rifampicin for the eruptive verruga peruana phase
Sandfly vector avoidance and control measures for prevention
Monitoring of haemolysis markers and haemodynamic status during the acute illness
Referral to infectious diseases or tropical medicine services
